name: Diego Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Calder Plumbing Supply, so I order the pipes, fittings and boiler parts that go out to plumbers' merchants. I'm in by seven, check what sold overnight in our old purchasing system, and ring or email suppliers when stock runs low. I only moved up from the warehouse floor two years ago, so I'm still learning, and Gwen, the senior buyer, double-checks my big orders. What wears me out is the supplier who promises Thursday and delivers the following Tuesday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what do you like least?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that a good order means plumbers get their parts and nobody on the van is standing around. I don't like the targets from Pieter, our head of purchasing, who wants stock cut by ten percent every quarter. My partner Marisol is a nurse at the city hospital, we've got Nico, eleven, and Ines, eight, and a mortgage on a terraced house off Alder Road, so I can't afford a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it be hype, because every time a company says software will save time, somebody ends up with a longer to-do list. At work I'd just shrug and keep ordering the way I always have. To friends I'd say the bosses love a shiny toy more than they love the people running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'm not totally relaxed even then. The company already tried an AI reorder tool last spring, it suggested daft quantities of copper elbows, and I ignored it. But somebody senior noticed it's cheap and I'm a junior with my feet barely under the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am and keep a spreadsheet of my own that shows what I caught that the tool didn't. I'd ask Gwen to put my name on the supplier negotiations so people see I'm more than a data-entry man. And I'd keep paying extra off the mortgage, about 200 a month, like we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit flat but fine. It's a normal-worry feeling, not a night-sweat one. Money is okay, but I know my job is the kind that gets tidied up first when somebody wants a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Pieter wants stock cut by ten percent. Does anything like that already sit in your mind when you hear AI is mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pieter's ten percent target comes up every quarter and I do feel it. If the AI tool turned out slightly useful, he'd probably use it as a stick to say my forecasts are guesswork. So even in a quiet world I'd feel watched. I'd rather be the man who knows the suppliers by first name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you say is to blame if it did go wrong at Calder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, the Hallows family, and Pieter, who passes pressure down and takes the credit. I wouldn't blame the software, it's just a thing. If they cut my hours I'd be asking why the family took a dividend that same year.

say: I'd say **good**, let it be hype, because software that saves time usually just adds work for somebody.
At work I'd **shrug** and keep ordering the way I always have.
think: I'm not fully relaxed, because the company already **trialled** an AI reorder tool and my seniors noticed it was cheap.
As a junior still learning, I'm the kind of **cost** that gets tidied up first.
do: Keep a **spreadsheet** of my own showing what I caught that the tool missed.
Ask Gwen to put me on supplier **negotiations** so I'm more than data entry.
Keep paying an extra **200** a month off the mortgage.
feel: A bit **flat**, but fine, a normal-worry feeling rather than a night-sweat one.
S0.quote: Every time a company says software will save time, somebody ends up with a longer to-do list.
fieldNote: Distrusts new tools on principle but knows his junior standing makes him easy to cut.
Blames owners and his boss, not the software itself.
Already carries a **mortgage** worry even when nothing changes.

steps.text: Keep ordering by hand and log every error the AI tool makes
Pay 200 a month extra off the mortgage
Ask to join the supplier negotiations with Gwen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a cost-cutting scheme dressed up as progress, and I'd say it loudly, because I've seen what happened to the old counter staff when the web shop arrived. At work I'd ask who checks the machine's orders when it gets them wrong. Online I'd post that if software takes the job, the company should pay a share of the saving into a fund for the people it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'm in the firing line. Booking, checking, comparing quotes, that's most of my day, and it's what the newspapers say AI does first. I'm the junior, two years in, no degree, and I know Gwen would survive and I might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union branch properly, I've only been a name on the list. I'd ask for our contract to say how many buyers there must be, and I'd put six months of wages into a separate account. I'd also take the warehouse supervisor's course on Saturdays, because that's work I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a tight feeling in the chest when I read the news. I'm not wild with panic because we have savings, about eight months of wages, but I know savings don't last when two incomes shrink. Marisol's hospital job is steady, which helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you ignore the AI tool now. What happens when it's not optional any more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to do it and I'd hate it. I'd probably be the slowest person on the team and Pieter would notice. I'd rather retrain than become the guy who types prompts badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marisol the night Pieter told you the buying team is shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, I'm going to keep us fed, we've got money put by, and we'll cut the holidays before we cut the kids' football. Then I'd call my cousin, who runs a depot, and ask about shift work. I'd say it calm, but I'd be awake till two.

say: I'd call it a **cost-cutting** scheme dressed up as progress and ask who checks the machine when it gets orders wrong.
I'd say the company should pay a share of the saving into a **fund** for the people it replaces.
think: Booking, checking and comparing quotes is most of my day, so I'm **in the firing line** as the junior.
Gwen would survive and I might not, with no degree and only two years in.
do: Join the union branch **properly** and push for a minimum number of buyers in our contract.
Move six months of wages into a separate **account**.
Take the warehouse supervisor's **course** on Saturdays.
feel: **Nervous**, with a tight chest when I read the news, but eased by our eight months of savings.
S1.quote: Booking, checking, comparing quotes, that's most of my day, and it's what the newspapers say AI does first.
fieldNote: Feels directly exposed: most of his day is the thinking work the card names.
Turns to the **union** and the warehouse, the world he came from, rather than to AI.
Savings and Marisol's hospital job keep this at anxious, not alarmed.

steps.text: Join the union branch and push for a minimum buyer headcount
Put six months of wages into a separate account
Take the warehouse supervisor course on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nobody's ready, not the company, not the union, not the government. I'd tell friends this is the moment for rules, a ban on firing people for software for a few years, and a tax on the companies that do it. I'd say it online too, but I'd probably get shouted at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: I'm done. Within two years a computer does my job better, cheaper, and doesn't take lunch breaks. Robots come around 2031 for the warehouse, so my old floor job is safe three years longer than my desk, which is a funny thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything extra, no new car, no holiday, no kitchen. I'd ask Pieter in writing what the plan is for buyers. I'd put every spare pound into the mortgage, and I'd go back to the warehouse and ask for my old picking shifts at least part-time, since the robots come later down there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. It's not a drama, it's a heavy feeling that sits in the stomach. Two years is not enough to retrain at forty-three with two kids, even with money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What changes for you compared with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old problem, that I'm a junior with no degree, becomes the main problem. Two years sounds like a deadline you can't negotiate with, and a slow decade I could have planned around. I'd have to decide quickly and I'm not good at deciding quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if your pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the holiday fund and the kids' clubs first, then the takeaways, then I'd look at the car payment. I'd leave the mortgage and the electricity till last. If it came to it we'd rent out the back room to a student.

say: I'd say nobody is ready, and we need a **ban** on firing people for software for a few years.
I'd push for a **tax** on the companies that replace staff with AI.
think: Within two years a computer does my buying job **better** and cheaper, so I'm done at my desk.
Robots reach the warehouse around 2031, so my old floor job is safe about **three** years longer.
do: Stop all **extra** spending: no car, no holiday, no kitchen.
Ask Pieter **in writing** what the plan is for buyers.
Ask to go back to part-time picking shifts in the **warehouse**.
feel: **Frightened**, a heavy feeling in my stomach, because two years is too short to retrain at 43.
S2.quote: Within two years a computer does my job better, cheaper, and doesn't take lunch breaks.
fieldNote: Sees his desk job as **gone** on the stated date and the warehouse as safe about three years longer.
The short warning, not the end point, is what scares him.
Cushion softens the panic but he expects to lose his income.

steps.text: Cut all extra spending: car, holiday and kitchen plans
Put every spare pound into the mortgage
Ask for part-time picking shifts back in the warehouse
Demand a written plan for buyers from Pieter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of time to waste if we don't act, and I'd say it to the union and the council. I'd say five years is long enough to build a proper retraining scheme and short enough that the government has to start this year. At work I'd keep my head down and say I'm learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit better than two years because I can plan, but it still ends in the same place. My desk goes in 2031, the warehouse jobs by 2034, and I'd rather not be fighting for those with everyone else who got laid off. I'd say five years is the difference between being pushed out and walking out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to finish the supervisor course and tell Pieter I'd like to move across to operations. I'd save about 400 a month instead of 200, and I'd ask Marisol if the hospital has porter or logistics jobs. I'd get involved with the union training fund, because somebody has to make them build one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit angry. I'm less scared because of the time, but angry that the plan seems to be to make ordinary workers adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives some room. Does that feel better or worse than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, definitely. Two years is a gun at your head, five is a mortgage term I can see the end of. But I don't trust that the company will give me a place in operations, so I'd be moving before they push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nico and Ines about the future of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them, learn to fix things, learn to talk to people, and don't think a screen job is safe. My eldest likes football and building Lego, so maybe engineering. I'd say it plain: be useful in a room with other people.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to build a proper **retraining** scheme, but only if the government starts this year.
At work I'd keep my head down and say I'm **learning**.
think: It's a bit better than two years because I can plan, but my desk still goes in **2031**.
I'd rather walk out than be **pushed**, so I'd move before the company decides for me.
do: Finish the supervisor **course** and ask Pieter to move me across to operations.
Ask Marisol whether the hospital has porter or **logistics** jobs.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit angry that ordinary workers are expected to do the adjusting.
S3.quote: Two years is a gun at your head, five is a mortgage term I can see the end of.
fieldNote: Time converts fear into planning but he still expects the desk job to go.
Anger is aimed at the system, which fits his union and public-support views.
Plans to move **before** being pushed, a real change for a man who prefers the familiar.

steps.text: Finish the supervisor course and ask to move into operations
Ask the union to start a retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair chance for everybody to get through it if governments plan. At work I'd say it's far off and keep ordering. To friends I'd say we should be voting for the people who build training schemes now, not the ones who say wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three, kids nearly grown, the mortgage close to done. It might even work out for me, if I'm already in operations by then. I'd still expect my buying desk to go, but I'd be old enough not to be wild about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and learn the supervisor ropes slowly, maybe one evening a week. I'd pay the mortgage down faster and not buy a bigger house. I'd also vote and write to my councillor about a retraining fund, because with ten years there's no excuse for nothing happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably okay, I'd say. Not happy, but I could live with it because I'd have time and money. The only thing that nags is that people say ten years and then nothing is ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Does it change how you'd spend this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend this year as usual, honestly. No panic, no big sale of anything, I'd just stop being so stubborn and start looking at what a supervisor really does. My dad worked thirty years at a bakery and never changed once, I'd like to change a little bit, on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the five-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into the mortgage and less into planning crazy moves. With five years I'd be pushing. With ten I'd let the union and the council do their bit while I do mine. I'd be the one in the room asking why the training fund hasn't started yet.

say: I'd say ten years is a fair chance if governments **plan**, and vote for people who build training schemes now.
At work I'd say it's far off and keep **ordering**.
think: I'd be 53 with the mortgage nearly done, so I could **live** with it if I'm in operations by then.
I still expect my buying desk to go, but I'd have **time** and money.
do: Learn the supervisor ropes **slowly**, one evening a week.
Pay the mortgage down **faster** rather than buying a bigger house.
Write to my **councillor** about a retraining fund.
feel: Reasonably **okay**, with one nag that people say ten years and nothing is ready.
S4.quote: My dad worked thirty years at a bakery and never changed once, I'd like to change a little bit, on my own terms.
fieldNote: Long runway lets him stay stubborn about tools but open about **moving** into operations.
Draws on his father's life, so his caution about change is rooted, not lazy.
Political action is his way of using the extra years.

steps.text: Study supervisor skills one evening a week
Keep paying down the mortgage faster
Write to the councillor about a retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It's the one where I haven't got time to change and Pieter can say sorry, it's the market. What would help is a law that makes the company keep people on while they retrain, and a union that can make that stick, plus a hospital job for Marisol that stays steady.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against new things, I'm against being the one who pays for them. If the company shares the saving, I'll learn whatever they like. I'd tell my kids the same, that fair is the point.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things, I'm against being the one who pays for them.
portrait: Diego is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Calder Plumbing Supply, promoted from the warehouse floor two years ago.
He's **union-minded**, distrusts new tools, and has never used AI; he ignored the company's reorder trial.
He's carrying a **mortgage** and two children, but has about eight months of wages saved and Marisol's steady hospital job.
His mood peaks at **alarmed** in the two-year world, and he turns to the union and warehouse, not AI.
He blames **owners** and his boss for passing risk down to workers.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because he can't retrain in time and the company could say it's just the market.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** making firms keep staff on while they retrain, with a union to enforce it.
